J. Jones , Yu Yuan , Sergio Maffeis View a PDF of the paper titled Speedbumps: Rejection Attacks on Speculative Decoding, by Adam Y. J. Jones and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Speculative decoding is a popular technique for increasing the speed and reducing the costs of large language model (LLM) inference by verifying multiple draft tokens in a single target-model forward pass. The resulting benefit depends on the ability of the drafter to approximate the target model's distribution. In this work, we study Speculative Rejection Attacks (SRAs), a novel class of attacks that cause draft and target models to disagree more often, resulting in fewer draft tokens being accepted per draft cycle. This leads to more target model forward passes needed per generated token, slowing down inference and increasing costs for the victim. We introduce two attacks which append an adversarial suffix to attacker-controlled content to degrade speculative decoding on a victim's prompts. Both attacks optimise the expected length of the accepted speculative prefix, estimating per-depth acceptance from the target's probability of the drafted proposals (Speedbump-P) or from the overlap between the draft and target distributions (Speedbump-D). In some cases, attacks degrade speculative decoding to the point of being slower than autoregressive decoding. The degradation reduces the output quality - regularisation restores output quality but gives up most of the degradation, trading effectiveness for stealthiness. Additionally, the suffixes remain effective under sampling, and transfer across drafters (Speedbump-P) or across target models sharing a drafter (Speedbump-D). These findings identify the draft-target interaction of speculative decoding as a realistic attack surface through which adversarial inputs can inflate inference costs. selected_records.title: Speedbumps: Rejection Attacks on Speculative Decoding

article.body:
Researchers describe attacks that can slow speculative decoding in language models

A paper submitted to arXiv on Oct. 7 describes two attacks designed to make large language models’ speculative decoding less efficient, potentially increasing inference time and cost for the system’s operator.

In “Speedbumps: Rejection Attacks on Speculative Decoding,” Adam Y. J. Jones, Yu Yuan and Sergio Maffeis call the methods Speculative Rejection Attacks. They append an adversarial suffix to attacker-controlled content in order to increase disagreement between a draft model and a target model. That disagreement means fewer proposed tokens are accepted in each decoding cycle, requiring more target-model processing to generate output, the authors say.

Speculative decoding speeds generation by having a drafter propose multiple tokens for a target model to verify in a single forward pass. Its benefit depends on how closely the drafter approximates the target model’s distribution, according to the paper’s abstract.

The two methods, named Speedbump-P and Speedbump-D, differ in how they estimate the likelihood that proposed tokens will be accepted. Speedbump-P uses the target model’s probability for the drafted proposals; Speedbump-D uses overlap between the draft and target distributions. The authors report that, in some cases, the attacks reduce performance enough to make speculative decoding slower than autoregressive decoding.

The paper also reports a trade-off between effectiveness and output quality: the attacks reduce quality, while regularisation can restore it but gives up most of the slowdown. The authors say the suffixes remain effective when generation uses sampling. They also report that Speedbump-P transfers across drafters, while Speedbump-D transfers across target models that share a drafter.

The authors present the findings as identifying the interaction between draft and target models as a way adversarial inputs could raise inference costs. The arXiv listing classifies the paper under cryptography and security and artificial intelligence.
